topic: What if your reaction time was ten times faster?
title: WHAT IF YOU
REACTED 10X FASTER?

power.rule: you react in 0.025 s instead of about 0.25 s: the world seems to slow while you move
power.look: time-slow: the world desaturates and slows, a SNAP chip and a stopwatch reading 0.025 s, a snap sound

script.text: A fly zips past your face. Snap. Caught it.
Your phone slips. Snap. Caught, mid-air.
A penalty, top corner. Snap. Saved. Every single one.
What if you reacted ten times faster?

script.beat: 4 the turn: the cost, one real fact
script.text: One catch. In a sprint, react faster than a tenth of a second and it's a false start. Too fast means disqualified. That's real.
And somebody in a black car just noticed.

science.claim: A normal visual reaction takes about 0.25 s; ten times faster is 0.025 s.
science.working: Typical simple visual reaction time is about 0.25 s (250 ms). 0.25 s / 10 = 0.025 s (25 ms). The stopwatch in the power's look reads 0.025 s.
science.source: Typical human simple visual reaction time (~250 ms); arithmetic

science.claim: In a sprint, reacting faster than a tenth of a second is a false start, and a false start means disqualification.
science.working: World Athletics rules treat a reaction time under 0.100 s from the gun, as measured by the start-block sensors (start information system), as a false start. Since 2010 one false start disqualifies the athlete responsible. 0.025 s is well under 0.100 s, so every start at that reaction time would be ruled a false start.
science.source: World Athletics Competition & Technical Rules, TR16.6 (reaction under 0.100 s = false start) and TR16.8 (one false start disqualifies, since 2010)

science.claim: Optional on-screen detail: a dropped ruler falls 30.7 cm in 0.25 s but only 3.1 mm in 0.025 s.
science.source: Free fall from rest, d = 1/2 g t^2 (standard gravity 9.81 m/s^2)
